title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Patient Safety & Infection Prevention
html:
Safe nursing care is built from repeatable habits: identify the correct client, notice hazards early, interrupt unsafe actions, prevent transmission, and reassess after every intervention. The RN does not wait for harm to occur before acting. Safety is an active clinical judgment process used during every encounter.

Learning goals

  • Use reliable safety checks before care, medications, procedures, and specimen collection.
  • Apply Standard Precautions to every client and add Transmission-Based Precautions when indicated.
  • Select hand hygiene and personal protective equipment from the anticipated exposure.
  • Protect a sterile field and respond safely to contamination, exposure, falls, and near misses.

Build safety into every encounter

Before an intervention, compare the client, order, allergies, procedure, equipment, and environment. Use at least two approved client identifiers according to organizational policy; a room or bed number is not a person-specific identifier. Resolve discrepancies before proceeding. Invite the client to state identifiers when possible rather than confirming information with a yes-or-no question.

Scan the environment for fall, equipment, electrical, medication, and mobility hazards. Keep needed items within reach, use prescribed mobility assistance, and communicate changes in risk. Restraints are not a routine fall-prevention strategy. Use the least restrictive safe approach and follow assessment, authorization, monitoring, and documentation requirements.

Safety sequence
Stop the unsafe action, protect the client from immediate harm, assess what happened, obtain appropriate help, communicate through the chain of command, and evaluate the response.

Standard Precautions: every client, every setting

Standard Precautions apply regardless of whether infection is known or suspected. They include hand hygiene; risk-based use of gloves, gown, mask, and eye or face protection; respiratory hygiene; safe injection and sharps practices; and appropriate cleaning, disinfection, sterilization, linen handling, and equipment reprocessing.

Perform hand hygiene immediately before touching a client, before an aseptic task, before moving from a soiled body site to a clean site on the same client, after contact with blood or body fluids, after touching the client or nearby environment, and immediately after removing gloves. Unless hands are visibly soiled, an approved alcohol-based hand rub is preferred in most clinical situations. Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled and whenever current policy or pathogen-specific guidance requires it. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

Select PPE from the exposure risk

  • Gloves: anticipated contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, nonintact skin, or contaminated material.
  • Gown: anticipated contamination of clothing or exposed skin.
  • Mask plus eye or face protection: anticipated spray or splash toward the nose, mouth, or eyes.
  • Respirator: required respiratory protection for airborne hazards according to current guidance, fit testing, and organizational policy.

Put on PPE before the exposure and remove it without transferring contamination to clothing, skin, or the environment. Perform hand hygiene after removal.

Add Transmission-Based Precautions

Contact, Droplet, and Airborne Precautions supplement—not replace—Standard Precautions for known or suspected transmissible infections. Contact Precautions emphasize barrier protection and dedicated or disinfected equipment. Droplet Precautions generally require a mask on room entry and source control for necessary transport. Airborne Precautions require appropriate respiratory protection and airborne-infection isolation placement when available. Begin indicated precautions from the clinical syndrome rather than waiting for a final laboratory result, then follow current pathogen-specific guidance and facility policy.

Protect the sterile field

A sterile field must stay dry, above waist level, continuously visible, and separated from nonsterile surfaces. The outer border of an opened sterile field is considered contaminated. Do not reach across the field. Moisture can carry microorganisms through a barrier, known as strike-through contamination. If sterility is uncertain or an item becomes contaminated, stop and replace the affected item or field.

When an event occurs

After a fall, equipment failure, medication variance, exposure, or near miss, address immediate needs and assess the client first. Notify the appropriate clinician or supervisor, follow required monitoring and reporting processes, and communicate unresolved risk. Chart objective client findings, care, notifications, and response. Complete a separate safety or incident report according to policy; do not use it as a substitute for the clinical record or document blame and speculation.

After a needlestick or blood or body-fluid exposure, promptly wash exposed skin with soap and water or flush exposed mucous membranes with water, then report immediately and obtain the designated post-exposure evaluation. Do not delay while finishing routine work.

Clinical example

Before collecting a blood specimen, the RN notices that the wristband date of birth does not match the order. The RN stops, keeps the client safe, and resolves the identification discrepancy through the approved process before collection. During the procedure, PPE is chosen from the splash risk, the sharp is discarded immediately in the designated container, hand hygiene follows glove removal, and the labeled specimen is checked at the point of care. Each small action closes a route to preventable harm.
